Proposition 9.3
On-path beliefs are pinned down by Bayes' rule
In any PBE, beliefs at information sets reached with positive probability are uniquely determined by the players' strategies via Bayes' rule. In a separating equilibrium (each type sends a distinct message), these beliefs are degenerate: observing a message reveals the sender's type with certainty. In a pooling equilibrium (all types send the same message), the on-path belief equals the prior — the message conveys no new information.

chunks.heading: Proof (Bayes' rule: turning observations into beliefs)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium & Believing What You See — 9.2 Proof (Bayes' rule: turning observations into beliefs)
chunks.body:
Apply Bayes' rule to each case. In a separating equilibrium, suppose the High type sends message $m_1$ with probability 1 and the Low type sends a different message $m_2$. Then $P(m_1 \mid H) = 1$ and $P(m_1 \mid L) = 0$, so
$$\mu(H \mid m_1) = \frac{1 \cdot P(H)}{1\cdot P(H) + 0 \cdot P(L)} = 1.$$
The belief is degenerate: $m_1$ reveals a High type for certain (and symmetrically $m_2$ reveals Low). The receiver learns the type exactly.
In a pooling equilibrium, both types send the same message $m_1$, so $P(m_1\mid H) = P(m_1 \mid L) = 1$ and
$$\mu(H \mid m_1) = \frac{1\cdot P(H)}{1\cdot P(H) + 1\cdot P(L)} = P(H).$$
The posterior equals the prior — the message is uninformative, exactly as intuition demands when everyone sends it. Any other message is now off-path (sent with probability zero), so Bayes' rule does not apply there and the belief is free to be chosen. ∎

chunks.heading: Worked example (Bayes' rule: turning observations into beliefs)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium & Believing What You See — 9.2 Worked example (Bayes' rule: turning observations into beliefs)
chunks.body:
Example 9.1
Reading a partial bluff
Suppose High and Low types are equally likely $(P(H) = P(L) = \tfrac{1}{2})$. The High type always sends message $m_1$, but the Low type sends $m_1$ only $30\%$ of the time (a partial bluff). On seeing $m_1$, what should the receiver believe?
By Bayes' rule:
$$\mu(H \mid m_1) = \frac{1 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}}{1\cdot\tfrac{1}{2} + 0.3\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}} = \frac{0.5}{0.65} = \frac{10}{13} \approx 0.77.$$
The receiver should believe there's about a $77\%$ chance the sender is High — up from the $50\%$ prior, because High types send $m_1$ more reliably. The message shifted the belief but didn't settle it, exactly as a poker bet narrows your read without confirming it.

chunks.heading: Signaling games, properly solved
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium & Believing What You See — 9.3 Signaling games, properly solved
chunks.body:
Now we can finish what Chapter 7 began. The job-market signaling story is a signaling game: Nature picks the sender's type, the informed sender chooses a message (education), and the uninformed receiver (employer) observes the message, forms a belief, and chooses an action (a wage). PBE is the right solution concept because the receiver acts at an information set — they see the message but not the type.
Nature draws the sender's type (High or Low, each $\tfrac{1}{2}$); the Sender (S) chooses Study or Slack; the Receiver (R) observes only the message and sets a wage. The gold dashed link and the belief labels $\mu$ mark the receiver's beliefs after each message. In this separating PBE the High type studies (belief $\mu = 1$, wage 20, net 15) and the Low type slacks (belief $\mu = 0$, wage 10, net 10); each type's payoff appears at the green leaves. Bayes' rule makes the beliefs degenerate, so the message reveals the type.

chunks.heading: Signaling games, properly solved
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium & Believing What You See — 9.3 Signaling games, properly solved
chunks.body: Take education to cost the High type 5 and the Low type 15 (single-crossing, as in Chapter 7), with a high wage of 20 and a low wage of 10. The separating PBE: High studies, Low slacks; the employer believes "studied ⟹ High" and pays accordingly. Check sequential rationality: the High type nets $20 - 5 = 15$ from studying versus 10 from slacking — studies. The Low type nets 10 from slacking versus $20 - 15 = 5$ from mimicking — slacks. Both beliefs follow from Bayes' rule. Every piece of the PBE definition is satisfied.

chunks.heading: The freedom of off-path beliefs
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium & Believing What You See — 9.4 The freedom of off-path beliefs
chunks.body: Here is where PBE reveals its subtlety — and its main limitation. In a pooling equilibrium, where both types take the same action, any other action is never observed in equilibrium. It is off the equilibrium path, reached with probability zero, so Bayes' rule is silent and the receiver's belief there can be anything. This freedom is what lets pooling equilibria survive.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (The freedom of off-path beliefs)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium & Believing What You See — 9.4 Theorem/Proposition (The freedom of off-path beliefs)
chunks.body:
Proposition 9.4
Off-path beliefs can sustain a pooling equilibrium
Suppose both types pool on the same message $m_1$. This is supported as a PBE if the receiver holds off-path beliefs at the unused message $m_2$ pessimistic enough that the resulting response makes deviation unprofitable for both types. Because Bayes' rule does not constrain off-path beliefs, such supporting beliefs can typically be found — which is precisely why PBE often admits many equilibria and motivates further refinements.

chunks.heading: Proof (The freedom of off-path beliefs)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium & Believing What You See — 9.4 Proof (The freedom of off-path beliefs)
chunks.body:
In a pooling PBE on $m_1$, on-path the receiver believes $\mu(H\mid m_1) = P(H)$ (the prior, by Proposition 9.3) and best-responds to that. Consider the unused message $m_2$. Since no type sends it in equilibrium, $m_2$ is reached with probability zero, and Bayes' rule places no restriction on $\mu(H \mid m_2)$.
Choose the off-path belief to be the most damning one — say $\mu(H \mid m_2) = 0$, i.e. "anyone who deviates to $m_2$ must be a Low type." The receiver then responds to $m_2$ with the action worst for the sender (the low wage). If even the type most tempted to deviate finds that the punishment response makes $m_2$ yield less than staying with $m_1$, then neither type deviates, and the pooling assessment is sequentially rational. Since the off-path belief was free to choose, this pessimistic belief is admissible, and the pooling equilibrium stands.

chunks.heading: Proof (The freedom of off-path beliefs)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium & Believing What You See — 9.4 Proof (The freedom of off-path beliefs)
chunks.body: The catch: nothing forces the off-path belief to be sensible. Refinements such as the Cho–Kreps intuitive criterion (1987) ask whether a deviation could only have come from a type that would benefit — and prune beliefs that ignore this. Such refinements often eliminate implausible pooling equilibria, sharpening PBE's predictions. ∎

chunks.heading: Key idea (The freedom of off-path beliefs)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium & Believing What You See — 9.4 Key idea (The freedom of off-path beliefs)
chunks.body:
Key idea
On the equilibrium path, Bayes' rule pins beliefs down. Off the path, PBE leaves them free — and a sufficiently pessimistic off-path belief ("only a low type would do that") can deter deviations and prop up a pooling equilibrium. This freedom is PBE's flexibility and its weakness, which is why refinements like the intuitive criterion exist.

chunks.heading: The refinement ladder
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium & Believing What You See — 9.5 The refinement ladder
chunks.body:
PBE sits on a ladder of ever-stricter solution concepts, each taming the one below by disciplining beliefs further. Nash equilibrium ignores sequence entirely; subgame perfection (Chapter 4) adds credibility within subgames; PBE adds explicit beliefs and Bayes' rule; sequential equilibrium (Kreps and Wilson, 1982) further requires off-path beliefs to be limits of beliefs from "trembles" — tiny mistakes — ruling out the most arbitrary ones; and the intuitive criterion prunes still more. Each rung trades a little simplicity for sharper, more credible predictions.
For most applied work — signaling, reputation, bargaining with incomplete information — PBE is the workhorse. It is exactly strong enough to make beliefs explicit and rational without the heavier machinery of sequential equilibrium, which is why it appears throughout modern economics.

chunks.heading: Open the arena
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium & Believing What You See — 9.6 Open the arena
chunks.body: Play the receiver and watch your belief bar move as Bayes' rule digests each message. Then play the sender and try to engineer a separating equilibrium — or hide in a pool and see what off-path belief the receiver would need to hold to tempt you out.

chunks.heading: Wrapping up
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium & Believing What You See — 9.7 Wrapping up
chunks.body: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium completes the logic of hidden-information games. By attaching an explicit belief to every information set, demanding sequential rationality given those beliefs, and tying on-path beliefs to Bayes' rule, it makes "what should I believe, and how should I act on it?" a precise question with a disciplined answer. We saw that separating equilibria reveal types through degenerate beliefs, that pooling equilibria hide them, and that the freedom of off-path beliefs both enables pooling and invites refinement. This closes the arc that began with signaling. Next, in Chapter 10, we return to a question we have so far dodged — what happens when no pure strategy is stable, and rational players must deliberately randomize.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.0 Overview
chunks.body: Every equilibrium so far has been a definite choice: cooperate or defect, enter or stay out, study or slack. But some games have no stable pure choice at all — whatever you settle on, your opponent can exploit. The escape is to stop being predictable: to randomize. This chapter shows why deliberate randomness is sometimes the only rational play, how to compute the right odds, and why every finite game has an equilibrium once we allow it.

chunks.heading: Story
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.0 Story
chunks.body: A tennis player stands ready to receive a serve. If she commits to guarding the left, a smart server aims right; if she leans right, the serve goes left. There is no single spot she should always cover — any fixed habit gets punished. Her best approach is to keep the server guessing: defend left some fraction of the time, right the rest, in proportions exactly calibrated so the server can't profit from aiming either way. Top players do this without naming it. Game theorists call it a mixed strategy.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.0 Overview
chunks.body: Penalty kicks, tennis serves, poker bluffs, tax audits, military feints — all share this structure. Predictability is fatal, so rational play requires randomization. Let's make the idea precise.

chunks.heading: When pure strategies fail: matching pennies
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.1 When pure strategies fail: matching pennies
chunks.body:
The cleanest example is matching pennies. Two players each secretly turn a coin to Heads or Tails. Player 1 (the "matcher") wins if the coins match; Player 2 (the "mismatcher") wins if they differ. The winner takes a point from the loser.
Try to find a stable pair of pure choices. If both play Heads, the matcher is happy but the mismatcher wants to switch to Tails. Once the mismatcher switches, the matcher wants to switch too. Chase this around and you find no pure-strategy resting point exists — every combination has someone wanting to deviate. The game has no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.
What does exist is a mixed strategy: a deliberate randomization over your pure choices.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (When pure strategies fail: matching pennies)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.1 Theorem/Proposition (When pure strategies fail: matching pennies)
chunks.body:
Definition 10.1
Mixed strategy
A mixed strategy for player $i$ is a probability distribution $\sigma_i$ over their pure strategies — a rule like "play Heads with probability $p$ and Tails with probability $1-p$." A pure strategy is the special case that puts all probability on one action. The support of a mixed strategy is the set of pure strategies it plays with positive probability. Payoffs are computed as expected values over the randomization.

chunks.heading: The indifference principle
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.2 The indifference principle
chunks.body: How do you find the right probabilities? The answer is a beautiful and slightly counterintuitive rule. When you choose your mixing odds, you don't pick them to make yourself better off across your options — you pick them to make your opponent indifferent. And in equilibrium, your opponent's odds make you indifferent. This is the indifference principle, the master key to every mixed equilibrium.

chunks.heading: Key idea (The indifference principle)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.2 Key idea (The indifference principle)
chunks.body:
Key idea
In a mixed-strategy equilibrium, each player randomizes in exactly the proportions that leave the other player indifferent among the strategies they're mixing over. If you're genuinely mixing between two actions, both must yield you the same expected payoff — otherwise you'd abandon the worse one. So your opponent's mix is pinned down by your indifference, and vice versa.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (The indifference principle)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.2 Theorem/Proposition (The indifference principle)
chunks.body:
Theorem 10.2
The indifference principle
If a player uses a mixed strategy in a Nash equilibrium, then every pure strategy in its support yields that player the same expected payoff (given the others' strategies), and no pure strategy outside the support yields more. Consequently, a player who randomizes over several actions must be exactly indifferent among them.

chunks.heading: Proof (The indifference principle)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.2 Proof (The indifference principle)
chunks.body:
Let player $i$'s mixed strategy $\sigma_i$ be a best response to the others' strategies, and suppose its support contains pure strategies that do not all give the same expected payoff. Let $a$ be a pure strategy in the support with the highest expected payoff $U_{\max}$, and $b$ one in the support with a strictly lower expected payoff $U_b < U_{\max}$.
The expected payoff of the whole mixture $\sigma_i$ is the probability-weighted average of the payoffs of the pure strategies in its support. Because $b$ is played with positive probability and earns strictly less than $a$, this average is strictly below $U_{\max}$. But then player $i$ could strictly increase their expected payoff by shifting all the probability weight from $b$ onto $a$ — contradicting the assumption that $\sigma_i$ was a best response.
Hence every pure strategy in the support must earn the same expected payoff. A pure strategy outside the support cannot earn strictly more, or shifting weight onto it would again improve the mixture. ∎

chunks.heading: Solving matching pennies
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.3 Solving matching pennies
chunks.body:
Now apply the principle. Let Player 1 play Heads with probability $p$ and Player 2 play Heads with probability $q$. We find each player's mix by making the other indifferent.
Player 2 (the mismatcher) is indifferent between Heads and Tails only if Player 1's mix makes both equally good. Working out Player 2's expected payoffs and setting them equal gives $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$. By the symmetric calculation, Player 1 is indifferent only if $q = \tfrac{1}{2}$. So the unique equilibrium is for both players to flip a fair coin — play Heads and Tails each with probability one-half.
We can see this equilibrium as the unique crossing point of the two players' best-response correspondences — the rules giving each player's optimal mix as a function of the other's.

chunks.heading: Solving matching pennies
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.3 Solving matching pennies
chunks.body: Each axis is a mixing probability: $p$ for Player 1's Heads, $q$ for Player 2's Heads. The violet path is Player 1's best response to each $q$ (match: go all-Heads when $q > \tfrac{1}{2}$, all-Tails when $q < \tfrac{1}{2}$); the amber path is Player 2's best response (mismatch: the opposite). The step-shaped correspondences cross at exactly one point, $(\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2})$ — the unique mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium, where each player is indifferent and neither can be exploited.

chunks.heading: Worked example (Solving matching pennies)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.3 Worked example (Solving matching pennies)
chunks.body:
Example 10.1
Rock-Paper-Scissors
Rock-Paper-Scissors has the same flavor: any predictable pattern loses. By symmetry, the equilibrium is to play each of the three actions with probability $\tfrac{1}{3}$.
Check the indifference principle. Against an opponent playing $(\tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3})$, any single move — say Rock — wins against one option, loses to one, and ties one, each a third of the time. Its expected payoff is
$$\tfrac{1}{3}(+1) + \tfrac{1}{3}(-1) + \tfrac{1}{3}(0) = 0,$$
and the same holds for Paper and Scissors. All three moves yield zero, so you are perfectly indifferent — exactly what the indifference principle demands. The uniform mix is the unique Nash equilibrium, which is why no fixed RPS strategy can beat a player who truly randomizes.

chunks.heading: Mixing in coordination games: Battle of the Sexes
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.4 Mixing in coordination games: Battle of the Sexes
chunks.body:
Mixed strategies aren't only for pure-conflict games. Consider Battle of the Sexes: two friends want to spend the evening together but disagree on where. Player 1 prefers the Opera, Player 2 prefers the Football match; both would rather be together at either venue than alone. There are two pure equilibria (both Opera, or both Football), but also a mixed one — capturing the genuine risk of a coordination failure.
With the natural payoffs (you get 2 at your preferred venue together, 1 at the other venue together, 0 if you end up apart), the indifference principle gives a mixed equilibrium in which Player 1 chooses Opera with probability $\tfrac{2}{3}$ and Player 2 chooses Opera with probability $\tfrac{1}{3}$.

chunks.heading: Worked example (Mixing in coordination games: Battle of the Sexes)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.4 Worked example (Mixing in coordination games: Battle of the Sexes)
chunks.body:
Example 10.2
The cost of miscoordination
In that mixed equilibrium, each player's expected payoff works out to $\tfrac{2}{3}$. Compare that to the pure equilibria, where the players earn $2$ and $1$. The mixed equilibrium is worse for both than either coordinated outcome.
Why would rational players land there? Because when each independently randomizes to hedge against the other's choice, they frequently miscoordinate — both insisting on their own favorite, or both deferring — and end up apart. The mixed equilibrium quantifies the real cost of failing to coordinate, which is why pre-play communication (agreeing where to meet) is so valuable: it selects one of the good pure equilibria over the lossy mixed one.

chunks.heading: Nash's great theorem: equilibrium always exists
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.5 Nash's great theorem: equilibrium always exists
chunks.body: Matching pennies had no pure equilibrium but did have a mixed one. Is that always true? In a one-page paper in 1950, John Nash proved the answer is yes — and it is the result that won him the Nobel Prize and made modern game theory possible.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (Nash's great theorem: equilibrium always exists)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.5 Theorem/Proposition (Nash's great theorem: equilibrium always exists)
chunks.body:
Theorem 10.3
Nash's existence theorem (1950)
Every finite game — any game with finitely many players, each having finitely many pure strategies — has at least one Nash equilibrium, possibly in mixed strategies.

chunks.heading: Proof (Nash's great theorem: equilibrium always exists)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.5 Proof (Nash's great theorem: equilibrium always exists)
chunks.body:
The argument is one of the most elegant in economics; here is its skeleton. Consider the set of all mixed-strategy profiles — one probability distribution per player. This set is compact (closed and bounded) and convex (a mix of two valid profiles is a valid profile), and it lives in a finite-dimensional space.
Define the best-response correspondence: a map that takes any strategy profile and returns the set of profiles in which each player best-responds to the others. A Nash equilibrium is precisely a fixed point of this map — a profile that is among its own best responses, so no one wants to move.
Nash showed this correspondence satisfies the hypotheses of Kakutani's fixed-point theorem: the best-response set is non-empty, convex (because expected payoffs are linear in one's own probabilities, so the set of best responses is a face of the simplex), and the correspondence has a closed graph (best responses vary "without jumps"). Kakutani's theorem then guarantees a fixed point exists — and that fixed point is a Nash equilibrium. Because the construction never required pure strategies, the equilibrium it delivers may be mixed. ∎

chunks.heading: Proof (Nash's great theorem: equilibrium always exists)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.5 Proof (Nash's great theorem: equilibrium always exists)
chunks.body: Nash's two-page argument generalized von Neumann's 1928 minimax theorem (which had guaranteed equilibrium only for two-person zero-sum games) to all finite games, cooperative or competitive, with any number of players. That leap is what turned game theory into a universal tool.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Nash's great theorem: equilibrium always exists)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.5 Key idea (Nash's great theorem: equilibrium always exists)
chunks.body:
Key idea
Allowing mixed strategies guarantees that every finite game has an equilibrium. A game might have no stable pure outcome (matching pennies), but it can never have no equilibrium at all. Nash equilibrium is therefore a universal solution concept — it always has something to say.

chunks.heading: Why randomness is rational
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.6 Why randomness is rational
chunks.body: A common objection: "Surely real people don't compute probabilities and flip mental coins." True — but the prediction still holds, for two reasons. First, in repeated competitive settings, any detectable pattern will be exploited, so survival pressure pushes skilled players toward unpredictability whether or not they reason it out. Studies of professional tennis serves and soccer penalty kicks find players randomize remarkably close to the game-theoretic proportions. Second, a mixed equilibrium can be reinterpreted: your opponent doesn't need you to actually randomize, only to be unpredictable from their vantage point — which a population of slightly different players, or your own private hesitations, can supply. Either way, the indifference conditions describe the stable resting point.

chunks.heading: Open the arena
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.7 Open the arena
chunks.body: The arena's AI tracks your move frequencies and transitions, so any bias — favoring Rock, or always switching after a loss — gets exploited. The only strategy it can't beat is the equilibrium mix. Try to feel how hard genuine randomness is for a human to produce.

chunks.heading: Wrapping up
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Mixed Strategies & the Power of Being Unpredictable — 10.8 Wrapping up
chunks.body: When no pure strategy is safe, rationality demands randomization. A mixed strategy spreads probability across your actions, and the indifference principle pins down the exact odds: you mix so as to make your opponent indifferent, and their mix makes you indifferent. Matching pennies settles at $(\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2})$, Rock-Paper-Scissors at the uniform mix, and even coordination games have mixed equilibria that measure the cost of miscoordination. Above all, Nash's existence theorem assures us that once mixing is allowed, every finite game has an equilibrium — game theory never comes up empty. In Chapter 11 we take this idea somewhere unexpected: into biology, where strategies aren't chosen by reasoning at all, but selected by evolution.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.0 Overview
chunks.body: Everything so far has assumed players who reason: who weigh payoffs, form beliefs, and choose. But what if no one is thinking at all? Evolutionary game theory makes a startling discovery — the logic of strategic equilibrium emerges even among organisms that never reason, driven by nothing but survival and reproduction. Strategies need no strategist. The same mathematics that describes a chess match also describes a meadow of competing wildflowers.

chunks.heading: Story
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.0 Story
chunks.body: In a population of animals contesting food, some are born aggressive — they escalate every fight — and some are born cautious, backing down to avoid injury. Neither type chooses its temperament; each simply inherits it and passes it on in proportion to how well it survives and breeds. If aggression spreads too far, aggressors mostly meet other aggressors and tear each other apart, so caution starts to pay. If caution spreads too far, a rare aggressor bullies everyone and prospers, so aggression creeps back. The population drifts toward a balance no individual designed — an equilibrium reached by dying and being born rather than by thinking.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.0 Overview
chunks.body: This idea, introduced by the biologist John Maynard Smith and George Price in 1973, transplanted game theory into biology and then back into economics and the social sciences. It replaces the rational chooser with a population of competing strategies, and rational best response with the blind arithmetic of reproduction.

chunks.heading: From rational choice to reproductive success
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.1 From rational choice to reproductive success
chunks.body: The reinterpretation is sweeping but simple. A strategy is no longer a deliberate plan but a heritable behavioral type — a phenotype, hardwired into an organism. Payoff is no longer utility but fitness: expected reproductive success. And instead of one player facing another, we imagine a large population in which individuals are repeatedly, randomly paired to interact, each earning fitness according to the encounter. Strategies that earn high fitness leave more offspring, so their share of the population grows.

chunks.heading: Key idea (From rational choice to reproductive success)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.1 Key idea (From rational choice to reproductive success)
chunks.body:
Key idea
Evolutionary game theory swaps the rational chooser for a population of inherited strategies, and best-response reasoning for reproductive success. A strategy "wins" not by being chosen but by leaving more copies of itself. Remarkably, the equilibria this blind process settles into are closely related to the Nash equilibria of the corresponding game.

chunks.heading: The evolutionarily stable strategy
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.2 The evolutionarily stable strategy
chunks.body: The central concept asks: which strategies, once common in a population, cannot be displaced by a rare alternative? A strategy that resists invasion by any mutant is evolutionarily stable.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (The evolutionarily stable strategy)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.2 Theorem/Proposition (The evolutionarily stable strategy)
chunks.body:
Definition 11.1
Evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS)
A strategy $s$ is an evolutionarily stable strategy if a population playing $s$ cannot be invaded by any rare mutant strategy $s'$. Formally, writing $E(a, b)$ for the fitness of playing $a$ against $b$, strategy $s$ is an ESS if for every mutant $s' \neq s$, either
(1) $E(s, s) > E(s', s)$ — the incumbent does strictly better against the population than the mutant does; or
(2) $E(s, s) = E(s', s)$ and $E(s, s') > E(s', s')$ — they tie against the population, but the incumbent does better against the rare mutants.

chunks.heading: The evolutionarily stable strategy
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.2 The evolutionarily stable strategy
chunks.body: The phrase to remember: an ESS is uninvadable. If almost everyone plays $s$ and a few mutants appear playing $s'$, the incumbents out-reproduce the mutants, and the mutation dies out. This is a refinement of Nash equilibrium tailored to populations: every ESS corresponds to a Nash equilibrium, but not every Nash equilibrium is evolutionarily stable. Evolutionary stability is the stricter, more demanding test.

chunks.heading: Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.3 Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint
chunks.body:
The founding example is the Hawk-Dove game, a model of conflict over a resource. Two animals contest a resource worth $V$. A Hawk escalates and fights; a Dove displays but retreats rather than risk injury. When two Hawks meet they fight, and the loser pays an injury cost $C$; when a Hawk meets a Dove the Hawk simply takes the resource; when two Doves meet they share it. The interesting case is when fighting is dangerous — $C > V$.
Is "always Hawk" evolutionarily stable? No. In a population of all Hawks, every contest is a costly fight, so the average Hawk does poorly — and a rare Dove, who never gets injured, does better by stepping aside. Doves invade. But "always Dove" isn't stable either: in a peaceful Dove population, a rare Hawk wins every encounter unopposed and spreads. The only stable outcome is a mixture — a precise balance of aggression and restraint.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.3 Theorem/Proposition (Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint)
chunks.body:
Proposition 11.2
The Hawk-Dove ESS
In the Hawk-Dove game with resource value $V$ and injury cost $C > V$, neither pure strategy is an ESS. The unique ESS is the mixed strategy that plays Hawk with probability
$$p^* = \frac{V}{C},$$
equivalently, a population in which a fraction $V/C$ of contestants behave as Hawks. At this mix, Hawk and Dove earn equal fitness, so the proportions stay put.

chunks.heading: Proof (Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.3 Proof (Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint)
chunks.body:
Use the standard payoffs: a Hawk meeting a Hawk earns $\tfrac{V-C}{2}$ (wins half the contests, pays the injury cost the other half); a Hawk meeting a Dove earns $V$; a Dove meeting a Hawk earns $0$; two Doves share, earning $\tfrac{V}{2}$ each.
Let the fraction of Hawks in the population be $p$. A Hawk's expected fitness is its payoff averaged over the opponents it meets:
$$E(\text{Hawk}) = p\cdot\frac{V-C}{2} + (1-p)\cdot V.$$
A Dove's expected fitness is
$$E(\text{Dove}) = p\cdot 0 + (1-p)\cdot \frac{V}{2}.$$
At an interior ESS the two types must earn equal fitness (otherwise the fitter type's share would grow and the mix would not be stationary). Setting $E(\text{Hawk}) = E(\text{Dove})$ and solving:
$$p\cdot\frac{V-C}{2} + (1-p)V = (1-p)\frac{V}{2}.$$
Expanding and simplifying, the $V$ terms collect to give $pC = V$, hence $p^* = \tfrac{V}{C}$. Because $C > V$, this lies strictly between 0 and 1, a genuine mixed strategy. One checks the ESS inequality holds: if the Hawk share rises above $p^*$, Doves become fitter and push it back down; if it falls below, Hawks become fitter and push it back up — so the mix is uninvadable. ∎

chunks.heading: Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.3 Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint
chunks.body:
The diagram shows the mechanism: the two fitness lines cross at exactly $p^* = V/C$, and the population is driven toward that crossing from either side.
With $V = 2$ and $C = 4$, Hawk fitness (rose) falls as Hawks become common — too many costly fights — while Dove fitness (teal) also declines but less steeply. They cross at the ESS $p^* = V/C = \tfrac{1}{2}$. To the left of the crossing Hawks are fitter, so their share rises; to the right Doves are fitter, so it falls. The population is pushed back to $p^*$ from either direction — the hallmark of evolutionary stability.

chunks.heading: Worked example (Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.3 Worked example (Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint)
chunks.body:
Example 11.1
Reading the Hawk-Dove balance
Take $V = 2$ (the resource) and $C = 4$ (the injury cost). The ESS hawk fraction is $p^* = V/C = \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2}$: half the contests are settled by aggression, half by restraint.
At that mix, a Hawk's fitness is $\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{2-4}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(-1) + 1 = \tfrac{1}{2}$, and a Dove's is $\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1 = \tfrac{1}{2}$ — equal, as required.
Now make fighting deadlier, $C = 8$: the ESS hawk fraction drops to $\tfrac{2}{8} = \tfrac{1}{4}$. Costlier conflict breeds more restraint — the model predicts that species with more dangerous weaponry evolve more ritualized, less lethal displays, exactly as biologists observe.

chunks.heading: Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.3 Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint
chunks.body: The ESS isn't a wholly new idea — it sits neatly inside one we already know. It sharpens Nash equilibrium rather than replacing it.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.3 Theorem/Proposition (Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint)
chunks.body:
Proposition 11.3
Every ESS is a Nash equilibrium
If a strategy $s$ is evolutionarily stable, then $(s, s)$ is a (symmetric) Nash equilibrium of the underlying game. The converse fails: there are symmetric Nash equilibria that are not evolutionarily stable. Thus ESS is a strict refinement of Nash equilibrium.

chunks.heading: Proof (Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.3 Proof (Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint)
chunks.body:
ESS implies Nash. The first ESS condition requires that for every mutant $s' \neq s$, $E(s, s) \geq E(s', s)$ — with strict inequality, or with equality backed by the tie-breaking second condition. In particular $E(s, s) \geq E(s', s)$ holds for all alternatives $s'$. But that statement is exactly what it means for $s$ to be a best response to itself: no deviation against an $s$-playing opponent does better. A strategy that is a best response to itself constitutes a symmetric Nash equilibrium $(s,s)$. So every ESS is a Nash equilibrium.
The converse fails. The even mix in Rock-Paper-Scissors, $(\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3})$, is a symmetric Nash equilibrium — every strategy earns the same payoff against it, so it is a best response to itself. Yet it is not an ESS: a mutant ties it on the first condition $(E(s,s) = E(s',s))$, and the required strict tie-breaker $E(s,s') > E(s',s')$ also fails, because the cyclic structure leaves the mix unable to out-compete invaders against themselves. Hence the population never settles — the cycling of Figure 11.2.

chunks.heading: Proof (Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.3 Proof (Hawk-Dove: the evolution of restraint)
chunks.body: So the ESS conditions are strictly stronger than Nash's: the second condition adds a stability requirement that pure best-response logic doesn't impose. Evolutionary stability demands not just that no mutant does better against the incumbents, but that the incumbents actively beat back the mutants. ∎

chunks.heading: The replicator dynamic: evolution as an equation
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.4 The replicator dynamic: evolution as an equation
chunks.body: The ESS describes where evolution settles. The replicator dynamic, introduced by Taylor and Jonker in 1978, describes how it gets there — the actual flow of the population over time. Its logic is the essence of natural selection in one line: strategies that do better than average grow; strategies that do worse shrink.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (The replicator dynamic: evolution as an equation)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.4 Theorem/Proposition (The replicator dynamic: evolution as an equation)
chunks.body:
Definition 11.4
The replicator equation
Let $x_i$ be the fraction of the population playing strategy $i$, let $f_i(x)$ be that strategy's current fitness, and let $\bar{f}(x) = \sum_j x_j f_j(x)$ be the population's average fitness. The replicator equation governs how the strategy shares change over time:
$$\dot{x}_i = x_i\,\bigl(f_i(x) - \bar{f}(x)\bigr).$$
A strategy's share grows when its fitness exceeds the average and shrinks when it falls below — selection in its purest mathematical form.

chunks.heading: The replicator dynamic: evolution as an equation
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.4 The replicator dynamic: evolution as an equation
chunks.body: Notice what this equation does not contain: no reasoning, no foresight, no choice. Just relative fitness. Yet its resting points — where $\dot{x}_i = 0$ for all $i$ — are Nash equilibria of the underlying game, and its stable resting points are closely tied to ESSs. Rationality, it turns out, is one route to equilibrium; selection is another, and they arrive at nearly the same place.

chunks.heading: Key idea (The replicator dynamic: evolution as an equation)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.4 Key idea (The replicator dynamic: evolution as an equation)
chunks.body:
Key idea
The replicator dynamic encodes natural selection in one equation: above-average strategies grow, below-average strategies shrink. It needs no rationality, yet its rest points are Nash equilibria and its stable rest points are ESSs — selection and reason converge on the same destinations. But "rest point" is not "stable": a population can sit at an equilibrium and still be blown off it by a single advantageous mutant.

chunks.heading: When evolution never settles: Rock-Paper-Scissors
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.5 When evolution never settles: Rock-Paper-Scissors
chunks.body:
Not every game has an ESS, and the replicator dynamic doesn't always converge. The vivid case is a population playing Rock-Paper-Scissors — found in nature among certain lizards whose mating types cycle exactly this way. Rock beats Scissors beats Paper beats Rock: a loop of cyclic dominance with no strategy on top.
The unique Nash equilibrium is the even mix $(\tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3})$ from Chapter 10 — but it is not an ESS. Under the replicator dynamic the population doesn't settle there; it cycles forever around it. When Rock is common, Paper invades and rises; as Paper grows, Scissors invades; as Scissors grows, Rock returns — an endless rotation.
Each point in the triangle is a population mix of Rock, Paper, and Scissors; the corners are pure populations. Under the replicator dynamic the state orbits the central Nash point $(\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3})$ in closed loops (green), never converging. Because Rock beats Scissors beats Paper beats Rock, whichever strategy is rising sows the seeds of the one that will overtake it. The Nash mix is an equilibrium but not an ESS — evolution here is perpetual motion.

chunks.heading: Why this matters beyond biology
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.6 Why this matters beyond biology
chunks.body: Evolutionary game theory's reach extends far past the meadow. In economics, firms that don't reason optimally but imitate successful rivals, or are selected by market survival, converge on the same equilibria as if they had calculated — a powerful defense of equilibrium predictions even when perfect rationality is implausible. In cultural evolution, norms, conventions, and fashions spread by imitation in exactly the replicator's "copy what's succeeding" pattern. The emergence of cooperation — why helping behavior survives despite the temptation to defect — is studied through evolutionary tournaments, where strategies like Tit-for-Tat (Chapter 3) prove robust over generations. And the framework explains stable polymorphisms throughout nature: why aggression and restraint, or multiple mating types, coexist in fixed proportions rather than one driving out the rest.

chunks.heading: Open the arena
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.7 Open the arena
chunks.body: Drag the injury cost up and watch the ESS shift toward more Doves in real time, or set unequal starting proportions and see the population flow back to the stable mix. Then switch to Rock-Paper-Scissors and trace the orbit as it loops around the center, never landing.

chunks.heading: Wrapping up
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Evolutionary Game Theory & Strategies Without Strategists — 11.8 Wrapping up
chunks.body: Evolutionary game theory shows that equilibrium does not require reasoning — only differential reproduction. An evolutionarily stable strategy is one no rare mutant can invade, a population-level refinement of Nash equilibrium; the Hawk-Dove game shows why conflict settles at a mix of aggression and restraint, with the ESS hawk-fraction $V/C$ falling as fighting grows costlier; and the replicator dynamic turns selection into a differential equation whose flow can converge to an ESS — or, as in Rock-Paper-Scissors, cycle forever. Strategies need no strategists. In the final chapter we turn the lens back on ourselves: Chapter 13 asks how real human beings play these games, and where they depart, revealingly, from every ideal we have built.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.0 Overview
chunks.body: Every game so far has been non-cooperative: players act alone, and any cooperation has to be self-enforcing. But sometimes players can sign binding agreements, form coalitions, and pool their gains — the only question is how to split the proceeds. Cooperative game theory steps back from individual moves and asks a different question: when a group creates value together, what division of the spoils is stable, and what division is fair?

chunks.heading: Story
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.0 Story
chunks.body: Three musicians can busk together. Alone, none of them draws much of a crowd. Any two of them together pull in a decent tip jar. All three, with harmony and a fuller sound, fill it to the brim. At the end of the night they tip out the jar — but how? Equal thirds feels fair until you notice the guitarist's solos are what stop people, or that any pair could have walked off and done nearly as well without the third. The money on the table is real; the puzzle is who deserves what, and which splits would actually hold together without someone storming off.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.0 Overview
chunks.body: This is the world of cooperative — or coalitional — games. We won't track individual strategies; instead we'll ask what each possible coalition can guarantee itself, and then seek principled ways to divide the total. Two ideas dominate the field: the core (which splits are stable) and the Shapley value (which split is fair).

chunks.heading: Coalitions and the characteristic function
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.1 Coalitions and the characteristic function
chunks.body: A cooperative game throws out the strategy tables and records just one thing: the value each group can create on its own.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (Coalitions and the characteristic function)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.1 Theorem/Proposition (Coalitions and the characteristic function)
chunks.body:
Definition 12.1
Coalitional game and characteristic function
A coalitional game (with transferable utility) consists of a set of players $N = \{1, \ldots, n\}$ and a characteristic function $v$ that assigns to every coalition $S \subseteq N$ a number $v(S)$ — the total payoff that the members of $S$ can guarantee themselves by cooperating, with $v(\varnothing) = 0$. The full set $N$ is the grand coalition, and $v(N)$ is the total value to be divided. An allocation is a vector $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ with $\sum_i x_i = v(N)$ specifying each player's share.

chunks.heading: Coalitions and the characteristic function
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.1 Coalitions and the characteristic function
chunks.body: "Transferable utility" means payoffs are like money — freely divisible and shiftable between players, so a coalition's worth is a single number it can split any way it likes. The characteristic function is the whole game: tell me what every coalition is worth, and the strategic problem becomes one of division.

chunks.heading: The core: which divisions hold together
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.2 The core: which divisions hold together
chunks.body: The first question is stability. A proposed split of the busking money is fragile if some subgroup could do better by walking off on its own. The core collects exactly the splits where no coalition has that temptation.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (The core: which divisions hold together)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.2 Theorem/Proposition (The core: which divisions hold together)
chunks.body:
Definition 12.2
The core
An allocation $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is in the core if it distributes the full value, $\sum_{i \in N} x_i = v(N)$, and no coalition can do better on its own:
$$\sum_{i \in S} x_i \;\geq\; v(S) \quad \text{for every coalition } S \subseteq N.$$
That is, every group receives at least what it could guarantee by breaking away. No coalition has a profitable objection, so the allocation is stable.

chunks.heading: The core: which divisions hold together
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.2 The core: which divisions hold together
chunks.body:
The core captures coalitional stability the way Nash equilibrium captured individual stability: in the core, no group — not just no individual — wants to deviate. Let's see what it looks like.
Every point in the big triangle is an allocation of the total value $v(N) = 1$ among three players; each corner gives everything to one player. For a symmetric game where every pair can secure $0.6$, the stability constraints $x_i + x_j \geq 0.6$ force each share below $0.4$, carving out the small green central triangle — the core. The Shapley value $(\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3})$ sits at its centroid, so here the fair split is also stable.

chunks.heading: When the core is empty
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.3 When the core is empty
chunks.body: A striking feature of the core is that it can be completely empty — there may be no stable way to divide the spoils. The cleanest illustration is a simple majority vote.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (When the core is empty)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.3 Theorem/Proposition (When the core is empty)
chunks.body:
Proposition 12.3
The majority game has an empty core
Consider three players dividing a prize of 1, where any majority (any two players) controls the whole prize: $v(S) = 1$ if $|S| \geq 2$ and $v(S) = 0$ otherwise. This game has an empty core — no allocation is stable.

chunks.heading: Proof (When the core is empty)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.3 Proof (When the core is empty)
chunks.body:
Suppose, for contradiction, that some allocation $(x_1, x_2, x_3)$ with $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 1$ lies in the core. Every two-player coalition can secure the whole prize, so the core constraints require
$$x_1 + x_2 \geq 1, \qquad x_1 + x_3 \geq 1, \qquad x_2 + x_3 \geq 1.$$
Add these three inequalities. The left side counts each player's share twice, giving $2(x_1 + x_2 + x_3)$, and the right side sums to $3$:
$$2(x_1 + x_2 + x_3) \geq 3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1 + x_2 + x_3 \geq \tfrac{3}{2}.$$
But the total to divide is only $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 1$, and $1 \geq \tfrac{3}{2}$ is false. The contradiction shows no core allocation exists. ∎
Intuitively: whatever the three agree to, some pair is getting less than the whole prize they could seize by themselves — so that pair always has an incentive to defect and cut out the third. Stable agreement is impossible. This is the mathematical heart of why shifting coalitions plague majority-rule politics.

chunks.heading: Key idea (When the core is empty)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.3 Key idea (When the core is empty)
chunks.body:
Key idea
The core is the set of allocations no coalition can improve upon — the stable splits. But the core can be empty: in a pure majority game, every division leaves some pair able to grab more by defecting, so no agreement holds. Stability is not guaranteed. (The Bondareva–Shapley theorem states exactly when a core exists: precisely when the game is "balanced.")

chunks.heading: The Shapley value: a formula for fairness
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.4 The Shapley value: a formula for fairness
chunks.body:
Stability and fairness are different questions. Even when many splits are stable (a fat core), which one is fair? And when the core is empty, we still need some principled division. In 1953 Lloyd Shapley answered both with a single formula, derived — like Nash's bargaining solution — from a short list of fairness axioms.
Shapley's idea: reward each player by their average marginal contribution — how much they add to a coalition by joining it — averaged over every possible order in which the players might assemble.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (The Shapley value: a formula for fairness)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.4 Theorem/Proposition (The Shapley value: a formula for fairness)
chunks.body:
Definition 12.4
The Shapley value
Imagine the players joining the grand coalition one at a time, in a random order (all $n!$ orders equally likely). Each player's marginal contribution is the extra value they bring when they join — the value of the coalition with them minus its value without them. The Shapley value $\varphi_i$ is player $i$'s marginal contribution averaged over all orderings:
$$\varphi_i(v) = \sum_{S \subseteq N \setminus \{i\}} \frac{|S|!\,(n - |S| - 1)!}{n!}\,\bigl[v(S \cup \{i\}) - v(S)\bigr].$$
The weights count the orderings in which player $i$ arrives right after exactly the players in $S$.

chunks.heading: The Shapley value: a formula for fairness
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.4 The Shapley value: a formula for fairness
chunks.body: Shapley proved this is the unique division satisfying four natural fairness requirements, in plain terms: efficiency (the whole value is distributed), symmetry (players who contribute identically get identical shares), the dummy property (a player who adds nothing to any coalition gets nothing), and additivity (the value of two combined games is the sum of the separate values).

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (The Shapley value: a formula for fairness)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.4 Theorem/Proposition (The Shapley value: a formula for fairness)
chunks.body:
Theorem 12.5
Shapley's theorem (1953)
There is a unique allocation rule satisfying efficiency, symmetry, the dummy property, and additivity: the Shapley value $\varphi$. In particular, the Shapley values always sum to the total worth, $\sum_{i \in N} \varphi_i(v) = v(N)$.

chunks.heading: Proof (The Shapley value: a formula for fairness)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.4 Proof (The Shapley value: a formula for fairness)
chunks.body:
We prove the efficiency property — that the Shapley values exactly distribute the total worth — using the "random order" description, which makes it transparent.
Fix any single ordering of the $n$ players, say they arrive as $\pi_1, \pi_2, \ldots, \pi_n$. As each arrives, credit them with their marginal contribution to the coalition already present. The first player gets $v(\{\pi_1\}) - v(\varnothing)$; the second gets $v(\{\pi_1,\pi_2\}) - v(\{\pi_1\})$; and so on. Summing these marginal contributions down the ordering, every intermediate term cancels with the next — the sum telescopes:
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n} \bigl[v(\{\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k\}) - v(\{\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_{k-1}\})\bigr] = v(N) - v(\varnothing) = v(N).$$
So in every ordering, the marginal contributions sum to exactly $v(N)$. The Shapley value of each player is their average marginal contribution across all $n!$ orderings. Averaging a collection of orderings whose totals are each $v(N)$ gives a total that is still $v(N)$:
$$\sum_{i \in N} \varphi_i(v) = \frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\text{orderings}} \underbrace{\bigl(\text{sum of marginals}\bigr)}_{=\,v(N)} = v(N).$$

chunks.heading: Proof (The Shapley value: a formula for fairness)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.4 Proof (The Shapley value: a formula for fairness)
chunks.body: Hence the Shapley value always divides the total worth completely — it is efficient. (Symmetry and the dummy property follow directly from the formula's structure; additivity holds because the formula is linear in $v$. Shapley's deeper result is that these four properties pin down this formula uniquely.) ∎

chunks.heading: Worked example (The Shapley value: a formula for fairness)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.4 Worked example (The Shapley value: a formula for fairness)
chunks.body:
Example 12.1
The glove market: scarcity is rewarded
Player 1 owns a single left glove; players 2 and 3 each own a right glove. A matched pair sells for $1$; an unmatched glove is worthless. So $v(\{1,2\}) = v(\{1,3\}) = 1$ (a pair can be formed), but $v(\{2,3\}) = 0$ (two right gloves, no pair), and any single player has $v = 0$.
Compute the Shapley value by averaging marginal contributions over all $3! = 6$ arrival orders. Player 1 (the scarce left glove) adds value in most orders; the interchangeable right-glove owners add value only when they arrive before the other right glove and after the left. Working through the six orderings gives
$$\varphi_1 = \tfrac{2}{3}, \qquad \varphi_2 = \tfrac{1}{6}, \qquad \varphi_3 = \tfrac{1}{6}.$$
The shares sum to $1$ (efficiency), and the scarce left glove captures two-thirds of the value while the two abundant right gloves split the rest. Scarcity is rewarded — a result that drops out of pure fairness axioms, with no bargaining assumed. (Interestingly, this game's core is the single point $(1,0,0)$: stability would hand the left-glove owner everything, so here the fair split and the stable split genuinely differ.)

chunks.heading: Key idea (The Shapley value: a formula for fairness)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.4 Key idea (The Shapley value: a formula for fairness)
chunks.body:
Key idea
The Shapley value pays each player their average marginal contribution across all orders of joining. It is the unique division satisfying efficiency, symmetry, the dummy property, and additivity — a formula for fairness. The core asks what is stable; the Shapley value asks what is fair, and the two answers need not coincide.

chunks.heading: Cooperative thinking in the world
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.5 Cooperative thinking in the world
chunks.body: The Shapley value is not just elegant — it is used. In cost-sharing, when several airlines share a runway whose cost depends on the largest plane, the Shapley value splits the bill so each airline pays its fair marginal share; the same logic divides the cost of a shared data center or a joint research facility. In politics, the closely related Shapley–Shubik index measures a voter's or party's power by how often they are the pivotal member who swings a coalition from losing to winning — revealing that voting power is not proportional to seats. In machine learning, "SHAP values" — a direct application of Shapley's formula — explain a model's prediction by fairly attributing it among the input features, treating each feature as a player in a cooperative game. And the core underlies the analysis of which trade agreements, partnerships, and matching markets are stable enough to last.

chunks.heading: Open the arena
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.6 Open the arena
chunks.body: Build the characteristic function yourself and watch the core shrink, shift, or vanish as you change what each coalition is worth. Then compare the Shapley value to the core — sometimes it sits comfortably inside, sometimes (as in the glove game) it lands well outside.

chunks.heading: Wrapping up
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Cooperative Games & Dividing the Gains Fairly — 12.7 Wrapping up
chunks.body: Cooperative game theory changes the question from "what will each player do?" to "how should a group divide what it creates?" The characteristic function records each coalition's worth; the core collects the stable divisions where no coalition wants to defect — though it can be empty, as the majority game shows; and the Shapley value delivers the unique fair division based on average marginal contributions, rewarding scarcity and pivotality. Stability and fairness are distinct goals that sometimes agree and sometimes clash. In Chapter 13 we close the book by turning from how players should behave to how they actually do — the findings of behavioral game theory, where real humans depart, systematically and revealingly, from the rational ideal.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.0 Overview
chunks.body: Twelve chapters have built an elegant theory of perfectly rational players. There is just one problem: people aren't perfectly rational. They care about fairness, they reason only a few steps deep, they make mistakes, and they punish unfairness at cost to themselves. Behavioral game theory takes the gloves off the laboratory and asks what humans actually do — and the gap between theory and behavior turns out to be not noise, but a deeper signal about human nature.

chunks.heading: Story
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.0 Story
chunks.body: A stranger is handed $10 and told to offer you some share of it. If you accept, you split it as proposed; if you refuse, you both get nothing. He offers you $1, keeping $9. Pure logic says take it — a dollar beats zero. Yet almost everyone in your position refuses, walking away with nothing rather than letting the stranger get away with such an insult. You have just paid a dollar to punish unfairness. Standard game theory says you blundered. Behavioral game theory says you did something deeply human — and that understanding why is essential to understanding real strategic life.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.0 Overview
chunks.body: That scenario is the ultimatum game, and the way people play it launched a revolution. Behavioral game theory, surveyed definitively by Colin Camerer in 2003, keeps the formal apparatus of the previous chapters but tests it against real human choices — and rebuilds the theory where the data demand it.

chunks.heading: The ultimatum game: fairness over money
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.1 The ultimatum game: fairness over money
chunks.body:
The setup is brutally simple. A proposer is given a sum, say $10, and offers some split to a responder. The responder either accepts (the split stands) or rejects (both get nothing). It is a one-shot, anonymous, sequential game — exactly the kind we solved by backward induction in Chapter 4.
What does our theory predict? Work backward. A rational, self-interested responder prefers any positive amount to zero, so they should accept even $1. Foreseeing this, a rational proposer offers the smallest possible positive amount and keeps the rest. The subgame-perfect prediction is stark: offer a penny, keep $9.99.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (The ultimatum game: fairness over money)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.1 Theorem/Proposition (The ultimatum game: fairness over money)
chunks.body:
Proposition 13.1
The self-interested ultimatum prediction
If both players are rational and care only about their own monetary payoff, the unique subgame-perfect equilibrium of the ultimatum game has the proposer offer the smallest positive amount and the responder accept any positive offer.

chunks.heading: Proof (The ultimatum game: fairness over money)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.1 Proof (The ultimatum game: fairness over money)
chunks.body:
Solve by backward induction, as in Chapter 4. Consider the responder's decision last. Faced with an offer of $x > 0$, accepting yields $x$ and rejecting yields $0$. Since a self-interested responder values only their own money and $x > 0$, accepting is strictly better; the responder accepts every positive offer. (At exactly $x = 0$ they are indifferent.)
Now the proposer, anticipating this, chooses the offer $x$ that maximizes their own retained share $10 - x$ subject to the responder accepting. Since any $x > 0$ is accepted, the proposer drives $x$ as low as possible — to the smallest positive unit (a penny) — and keeps essentially the whole pie.
This is the unique subgame-perfect equilibrium under pure self-interest. It is logically airtight — and almost nobody plays it. The failure is not in the mathematics but in the assumption that people value only their own money. ∎

chunks.heading: The ultimatum game: fairness over money
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.1 The ultimatum game: fairness over money
chunks.body: Now the data. Across thousands of experiments and dozens of cultures, the actual behavior is dramatically different: proposers typically offer 40-50% of the pie, and responders routinely reject offers below about 30%, choosing nothing over a lopsided split. The clean theory is decisively rejected — not by a little, but at the heart of its prediction.

chunks.heading: Key idea (The ultimatum game: fairness over money)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.1 Key idea (The ultimatum game: fairness over money)
chunks.body:
Key idea
The ultimatum game cleanly separates self-interest from fairness. Pure self-interest predicts "offer almost nothing, accept almost anything." Real people offer near-even splits and reject unfair ones at personal cost. The deviation is large, systematic, and cross-cultural — evidence that human payoffs include fairness and reciprocity, not just money.

chunks.heading: Social preferences: payoffs beyond money
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.2 Social preferences: payoffs beyond money
chunks.body:
The fix is not to abandon game theory but to enrich the payoffs. People act as if their utility depends not only on their own material reward but also on how it compares to others' — a phenomenon called inequity aversion, modeled influentially by Fehr and Schmidt in 1999. A responder who suffers a fairness penalty from a lopsided split will reject it when that penalty outweighs the money on offer; the rejection is perfectly rational once fairness is in the utility function.
These social preferences — caring about fairness, reciprocity, others' welfare — explain a whole family of experimental findings: generosity in the dictator game, trust and repayment in the trust game, and cooperation in public-goods games sustained by costly punishment of free-riders. The lesson is subtle: people are not irrational; they are optimizing a richer objective than the textbook assumed.

chunks.heading: Bounded reasoning: the level-k model
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.3 Bounded reasoning: the level-k model
chunks.body:
Fairness explains the ultimatum game, but a second, distinct departure concerns how deeply people reason about others. Equilibrium analysis assumes everyone thinks through everyone else's reasoning, infinitely deep. Real people stop after a step or two. The cleanest demonstration is the beauty contest game.
Everyone picks a number from 0 to 100. The winner is whoever comes closest to $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of the average of all guesses. What's the equilibrium? If everyone is fully rational and knows everyone else is, the only Nash equilibrium is everyone picks 0: whatever the average, you want two-thirds of it, which pulls every best response downward until the only consistent point is zero. Yet almost no one picks 0.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (Bounded reasoning: the level-k model)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.3 Theorem/Proposition (Bounded reasoning: the level-k model)
chunks.body:
Definition 13.2
Level-k reasoning
In the level-k model, players differ in their depth of strategic reasoning. A level-0 player acts naively or randomly (in the beauty contest, guessing around the midpoint 50). A level-1 player best-responds to the belief that everyone else is level-0. A level-2 player best-responds to a population of level-1 players, and so on. Most people are level 1 or 2 — they reason a step or two about others, but not to the infinite depth equilibrium requires.

chunks.heading: Bounded reasoning: the level-k model
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.3 Bounded reasoning: the level-k model
chunks.body:
Trace it through. A level-0 guess anchors at 50. A level-1 player assumes others guess 50 and picks $\tfrac{2}{3} \times 50 \approx 33$. A level-2 player assumes others are level-1 and picks $\tfrac{2}{3} \times 33 \approx 22$. Each extra step of reasoning multiplies the guess by $\tfrac{2}{3}$, marching toward the Nash equilibrium of 0 — but real populations stop early.
Each level of reasoning multiplies the guess by $\tfrac{2}{3}$: a level-0 anchor of 50 becomes 33 at level 1, 22 at level 2, and so on, converging to the Nash equilibrium of 0 only in the limit of infinite reasoning. Experimentally (Nagel, 1995), winning numbers cluster around 20-35 — exactly where one or two levels of reasoning land. Almost no one plays the equilibrium, because almost no one reasons infinitely deep.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (Bounded reasoning: the level-k model)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.3 Theorem/Proposition (Bounded reasoning: the level-k model)
chunks.body:
Proposition 13.3
Level-k guesses converge to Nash
In the $\tfrac{2}{3}$-beauty contest, a level-$k$ player anchored at 50 guesses $50 \cdot \left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^k$. As the reasoning depth $k \to \infty$, this converges to $0$, the unique Nash equilibrium. Finite reasoning yields guesses strictly above 0, matching observed behavior.

chunks.heading: Proof (Bounded reasoning: the level-k model)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.3 Proof (Bounded reasoning: the level-k model)
chunks.body:
By definition a level-0 player guesses the anchor $g_0 = 50$. A level-1 player believes everyone is level-0, so believes the average will be 50, and best-responds by guessing two-thirds of it: $g_1 = \tfrac{2}{3}\cdot 50$. A level-2 player believes everyone is level-1, expects the average to be $g_1$, and guesses $g_2 = \tfrac{2}{3} g_1 = \left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 50$. By induction, a level-$k$ player guesses
$$g_k = 50 \cdot \left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^{k}.$$
Since the common ratio $\tfrac{2}{3}$ satisfies $0 < \tfrac{2}{3} < 1$, this geometric sequence converges to $0$ as $k \to \infty$:
$$\lim_{k \to \infty} 50\left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^k = 0.$$
The limit $0$ is exactly the Nash equilibrium reached by iterated elimination of dominated strategies (no guess above $\tfrac{2}{3}\cdot 100$ can ever win, then none above $\left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 100$, and so on down to 0). So full rationality corresponds to infinite reasoning depth — the $k \to \infty$ limit — while any finite level gives a strictly positive guess. Since experimental subjects reason only a step or two, their guesses land well above zero, near $g_1$ and $g_2$. ∎

chunks.heading: Key idea (Bounded reasoning: the level-k model)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.3 Key idea (Bounded reasoning: the level-k model)
chunks.body:
Key idea
Nash equilibrium assumes infinite depth of reasoning — everyone thinks about everyone thinking, without end. The level-k model says real people stop after one or two steps. This explains why equilibrium predictions are systematically off in games solved by deep iteration, and why "thinking one step ahead of the crowd" — not infinitely ahead — is often the winning move.

chunks.heading: Learning, mistakes, and quantal response
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.4 Learning, mistakes, and quantal response
chunks.body:
Two further refinements round out the behavioral picture. First, people learn: in repeated play, behavior often drifts toward equilibrium as players adjust to experience, even if first-round play is far off. The beauty contest, replayed, sees guesses fall round after round toward 0 — reasoning depth effectively increases with feedback. Second, people make mistakes, and better options are chosen more often but not exclusively. The quantal response equilibrium (McKelvey and Palfrey, 1995) formalizes this: instead of always best-responding, players choose better actions with higher probability, so a little noise blurs the sharp edges of equilibrium. This single idea explains many small, systematic deviations that pure Nash analysis treats as error.
Together, social preferences, bounded reasoning, learning, and choice noise turn game theory from a theory of idealized agents into a far more accurate — and more useful — account of real strategic behavior, without discarding the elegant scaffolding the earlier chapters built.

chunks.heading: Open the arena
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.5 Open the arena
chunks.body: Make ultimatum offers and feel the tension between greed and the fear of rejection; play responder and decide how much unfairness you'll tolerate. Then set the AI's reasoning depth in the beauty contest and discover the uncomfortable truth: to win, you want to be exactly one level above the crowd — no more.

chunks.heading: Wrapping up — and looking back
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Behavioral Game Theory & How People Actually Play — 13.6 Wrapping up — and looking back
chunks.body: Behavioral game theory closes the loop between theory and reality. The ultimatum game shows that people value fairness enough to punish unfairness at a cost, captured by social preferences and inequity aversion. The beauty contest and the level-k model show that people reason only a step or two deep, not to the infinite depth equilibrium assumes. Learning and quantal-response noise fill in the rest. None of this discards the previous twelve chapters — it enriches their payoffs and bounds their rationality, turning a beautiful idealization into a working science of human strategy. You now hold the whole arc: from dominant strategies and Nash equilibrium, through sequential and repeated play, hidden information, randomization, evolution, and cooperation, to the behavior of real people. The final chapter adds the calculus that powers the continuous-strategy models at the frontier of economics.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Continuous Strategies: Calculus Applications — 14.0 Overview
chunks.body: Every game so far has had a handful of discrete choices. But the most powerful applications of game theory in economics live in the continuous world — where a firm sets any quantity or price, a shop picks any location, a contestant exerts any level of effort. Here strategies are real numbers, best responses become functions, and the tool for finding equilibrium is calculus. This capstone applies the first-order condition to the classic models that built modern industrial economics.

chunks.heading: Story
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Continuous Strategies: Calculus Applications — 14.0 Story
chunks.body: Two factories make the same steel. Neither posts a price or a fixed output; each morning the manager decides how many tons to roll, knowing the rival is deciding too, and knowing the market price will sag if together they flood the market. There is no short list of options to compare — output is a dial that turns smoothly from zero to the capacity of the plant. To find the resting point of this game, counting payoffs in a table is hopeless. You need the one move from calculus that finds the top of any smooth hill: set the derivative to zero.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Continuous Strategies: Calculus Applications — 14.0 Overview
chunks.body: That single move — the first-order condition — unlocks the whole chapter. When a player's strategy is a continuous variable and their payoff is a smooth function of it, the best response is found by differentiating the payoff with respect to one's own choice and setting it to zero. Do that for each player, solve the resulting equations together, and you have the Nash equilibrium. We'll apply this recipe to six landmark models.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Continuous Strategies: Calculus Applications — 14.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
Key idea
When strategies are continuous, the Nash equilibrium recipe becomes calculus: for each player, differentiate their payoff with respect to their own strategy, holding rivals' choices fixed, and set the derivative to zero. This first-order condition gives each player's reaction function (best response to the others). Solving all the reaction functions simultaneously yields the equilibrium.

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Continuous Strategies: Calculus Applications — 14.0 Theorem/Proposition
chunks.body:
Definition 14.1
Reaction function and the first-order condition
For a player with continuous strategy $s_i$ and payoff $\pi_i(s_i, s_{-i})$ that is smooth and concave in $s_i$, the best response solves the first-order condition
$$\frac{\partial \pi_i}{\partial s_i} = 0.$$
The solution, written as a function of the rivals' strategies $s_{-i}$, is the player's reaction function (or best-response function) $s_i = R_i(s_{-i})$. A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile where every player is on their reaction function simultaneously — the solution of the system of first-order conditions. (The partial derivative $\partial \pi_i / \partial s_i$ means differentiate with respect to $s_i$ while treating the rivals' choices as constants.)

chunks.heading: Cournot competition: choosing quantities
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Continuous Strategies: Calculus Applications — 14.1 Cournot competition: choosing quantities
chunks.body:
The first and most famous continuous game, due to Antoine Cournot in 1838 — decades before game theory had a name — has firms competing by choosing quantities. Two firms produce an identical good. The market price falls as total output rises, according to the inverse demand $P = a - bQ$, where $Q = q_1 + q_2$ is total output. Each firm has constant marginal cost $c$ and chooses its own quantity to maximize profit, taking the rival's quantity as given.
Firm 1's profit is revenue minus cost:
$$\pi_1 = \bigl(a - b(q_1 + q_2) - c\bigr)\,q_1.$$

chunks.heading: Theorem/Proposition (Cournot competition: choosing quantities)
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Continuous Strategies: Calculus Applications — 14.1 Theorem/Proposition (Cournot competition: choosing quantities)
chunks.body:
Proposition 14.2
The Cournot equilibrium
